The retrieved documents provide complementary information about roofing materials: d1, d2, d3, d5, d6, and d8 each list multiple common materials (asphalt shingles, metal, wood, tile, rubber/EPDM, built-up roofing, steel/aluminum, thatch, etc.), focusing on different aspects like popularity, cost, application (flat vs pitched roofs), historical use, or regional examples. None contradicts another; they collectively expand the answer by covering diverse materials and contexts.

The evidence together yields a comprehensive answer: asphalt shingles are widely cited as the most common modern material [d1][d2][d6], while many other materials like metal, wood, clay/concrete tile, rubber (EPDM), built-up roofing, and steel are also used, depending on roof type, climate, cost, and historical or regional practices [d1][d3][d5][d7][d8]. Each document adds a distinct set of examples without conflict, fitting the complementary-information label.

Roofs of houses are built with a variety of materials. Asphalt shingles are the most popular roofing material in North America, made from a fiberglass base topped with asphalt and mineral granules [d1][d2]. Other common materials include metal roofing (steel or aluminum) [d5], clay or concrete tiles (often for Spanish-style houses) [d3], wood shakes or shingles [d1], and synthetic membranes like EPDM rubber for flat roofs [d1][d3]. Historically, materials like clay tiles, thatch, and slate have also been used [d7][d8]. The choice depends on roof type, climate, cost, and architectural style.
